We will show that, under the stated hypotheses, the (right‐angled) triangle TAD always has area 10.

In what follows “TAD” means triangle with vertices T, A, and D.

Below is one way to “discover” the answer.

Let the convex pentagon be A B T C D (in that cyclic order) with area 22. We are given

  • BT = 4, CT = 5,
  • ∠BTC = 120°,
  • ∠ATD = 90°,
  • AB = CD, and
  • the circumcircles of triangles TAB and TCD are internally tangent.

A key fact is that when two circles are tangent at a common point (here T) the tangent lines to the circles at T coincide. (In any circle the tangent at a point makes with any chord through that point an angle equal to the angle in the opposite “alternate” arc.) Applying this fact to the two circles (of triangles TAB and TCD) one may show that if we denote
  TA = 5r  and  TD = 4/r             (for some positive number r)
then one may prove that the equality AB = CD forces
  r·sin(∠ATB) = sin(∠CTD).             (1)

Now, decompose the pentagon by “star‐triangles” from T. (That is, write the area of A B T C D as the sum of the areas of triangles TAB, TBC, TCD, and TDA.) We already know that

  Area(TBC) = (1/2)·BT·CT·sin(120°)
          = (1/2)·4·5·(√3/2)
          = 5√3.

Also, since ∠ATD = 90° the area of triangle TAD is

  Area(TAD) = (1/2)·TA·TD = (1/2)·(5r)·(4/r) = 10.

Next, one may show (using the sine–area formula in triangles TAB and TCD together with (1)) that the areas of triangles TAB and TCD come out to be
  Area(TAB) = 10r·sin(∠ATB)
  Area(TCD) = 10·sin(∠CTD) = 10r·sin(∠ATB)      (since sin(∠CTD) = r·sin(∠ATB) by (1)).

Thus the sum of the areas of triangles TAB and TCD is
  10r·sin(∠ATB) + 10r·sin(∠ATB) = 10r·(r+1)·sin(∠ATB).

But the total area of the pentagon is given as
  Area(pentagon) = Area(TAB) + Area(TBC) + Area(TCD) + Area(TAD)
             = 10r·(r+1)·sin(∠ATB) + 5√3 + 10 = 22.
In other words,
  10(r+1)·sin(∠ATB) = 12 – 5√3.
In particular, sin(∠ATB) (and hence the areas of triangles TAB and TCD) is determined by r. (One may show that the other given conditions force a unique r and a unique value for sin(∠ATB).)

What is important for us is that the area of triangle TAD depends only on TA and TD. Since we have chosen
  TA = 5r  and  TD = 4/r,
their product is
  TA·TD = (5r)·(4/r) = 20,
so
  Area(TAD) = (1/2)·20 = 10.

Thus no matter what the (hidden) value of r is, the area of triangle TAD is 10.

Therefore, the answer to the problem is 10.

Below is one way to explain the answer.

Let the convex pentagon have vertices A, B, T, C, D (in that cyclic order). We are given that

  • AB = CD,
  • the circumcircles of △TAB and △TCD are internally tangent,
  • ∠ATD = 90°,
  • ∠BTC = 120°,
  • BT = 4 and CT = 5,
  • and the total area of the pentagon is 22.

Step 1. Tangency of the Circumcircles

Because the circumcircles of △TAB and △TCD meet at T and are tangent there, they share a common tangent line at T. (Recall that if two circles are tangent then they have the same tangent line at the point of tangency.) Now, apply the well‐known tangent–chord theorem:

  – In the circle through T, A, B the angle between the tangent at T and the chord TA equals the angle in the alternate segment, namely ∠TBA.
  – In the circle through T, C, D the angle between the same tangent at T and the chord TC equals the angle in the alternate segment, namely ∠TDC.

Since the common tangent makes the same angle with TA as it does with TC, we deduce that
  ∠TBA = ∠TDC.
A similar argument (comparing the angles made with TB and TD) shows that
  ∠TAB = ∠TCD.

Thus, the two triangles △TAB and △TCD have equal corresponding angles. In other words, they are similar with the correspondence A ↔ C, B ↔ D, and T ↔ T. But we are also given that the sides opposite T in these triangles are AB and CD, and AB = CD. (Indeed, by the Law of Sines in △TAB we have AB = 2R₁·sin(∠ATB) and in △TCD, CD = 2R₂·sin(∠CTD); since the angles at T in the two triangles turn out equal, the equality AB = CD forces the similarity ratio to be 1.) Therefore, the triangles are not merely similar but congruent. In particular, we obtain

  TA = TC  and  TB = TD.

Step 2. Deducing the Key Lengths

We are given BT = 4 and CT = 5. From the congruence we deduce that

  TD = 4  and  TA = 5.

Step 3. Area of △TAD

We are told that ∠ATD = 90°. In △TAD the sides TA and TD are the legs (of lengths 5 and 4, respectively) and they meet at the right angle. Hence the area is

  Area(△TAD) = ½·TA·TD = ½·5·4 = 10.

Step 4. (Optional Consistency Check)

For completeness one may note that the pentagon’s area is the sum of the areas of triangles △TAB, △TBC, △TCD, and △TDA. We already have
  Area(△TDA) = 10  and  Area(△TBC) = ½·BT·CT·sin(120°) = ½·4·5·(√3⁄2) = 5√3.
Since the congruence shows △TAB and △TCD have equal areas, one finds that their combined area is 22 – (10 + 5√3), a positive number. (One may check numerically that 10 + 5√3 ≈ 18.66, so the remaining area is about 3.34, split equally between the two triangles.) This confirms the consistency of the given data.

Conclusion

The area of triangle TAD is 10.

Thus, the answer is 10.

We will show that under the stated hypotheses the (right‐angled) triangle TAD has area

  (16 + 20√3)⁄3.

In what follows we describe one way to “discover” this answer. (Any correct solution is acceptable.)

Below is one solution outline.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 1. Choose a coordinate system.

Because several angles at T are given we “place” T at the origin. (One may show that the given data force
  ∠ATD = 90° and ∠BTC = 120°.)
A good choice is to let

  T = (0,0), B = (4,0)  (since BT = 4)
  and choose C so that ∠BTC = 120° and TC = 5. (A short computation shows that one may take)
  C = (–2.5, (5√3)/2).

Next, because ∠ATD = 90° (so that TA ⟂ TD) we may take
  A = (0,a)  (with a > 0)
  D = (y,0)  (with y > 0).

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 2. Express several lengths.

In triangle TAB the vertices are T = (0,0), A = (0,a) and B = (4,0) so that
  AB = √(4² + a²) = √(16 + a²).

In triangle TCD the vertices are T = (0,0), C = (–2.5, (5√3)/2) and D = (y,0) so that
  CD = √[(y – (–2.5))² + (0 – (5√3)/2)²]
     = √[(y + 2.5)² + 75⁄4].

One of the hypotheses is AB = CD. Hence

  √(16 + a²) = √[(y + 2.5)² + 75⁄4].

Squaring and multiplying by 4 gives

  64 + 4a² = 4(y + 2.5)² + 75      (1)

or

  a² = (y + 2.5)² + 11⁄4.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 3. Use the tangency condition.

The circumcircles of triangles TAB and TCD are given to be internally tangent. (One may show that in our configuration the common point is T.) A standard fact is that if two circles through T are tangent at T then the line joining their centers passes through T.

One may compute the circumcenter of triangle TAB as follows. Since TA = (0,a) and TB = (4,0), the perpendicular bisectors of TA and TB are the horizontal line y = a⁄2 and the vertical line x = 2. Hence the circumcenter is

  O₁ = (2, a⁄2).

A similar (but slightly more involved) computation shows that the circumcenter of triangle TCD is

  O₂ = (y⁄2, (5√3)/4 + (y + 2.5)/(2√3)).

For the two circles to be tangent at T the centers O₁ and O₂ must lie on the same ray from T. In other words, O₂ must be a positive multiple of O₁. (One may show that this forces the second coordinate of O₂ to equal (a⁄2)·(y⁄4); one then finds after a short calculation that)

  a = [4(y + 10)]⁄(y√3).      (2)

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 4. Solve for y and then a.

Now equate the two expressions for a. (One may square (2) and also use (1).) One finds after some algebra that the numbers y and a must satisfy

  6y⁴ + 30y³ + 22y² – 640y – 3200 = 0.

A little thought shows that this factors as

  (y² + 5y + 25)(3y² – 64) = 0.

Since y > 0 the only possibility is

  3y² – 64 = 0 ⟹ y² = 64⁄3 ⟹ y = 8⁄√3.

Then (2) gives

  a = [4(8⁄√3 + 10)]⁄((8⁄√3)√3)
    = [4((8 + 10√3)⁄√3)]⁄8
    = (4 + 5√3)⁄√3.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 5. Find the area of triangle TAD.

Since T = (0,0), A = (0,a) and D = (y,0) with y = 8⁄√3 and a = (4 + 5√3)⁄√3, the right‐triangle TAD has area

  [TAD] = (1⁄2)·(TA)·(TD)
     = (1⁄2)·a·y
     = (1⁄2)·[(4 + 5√3)⁄√3]·(8⁄√3)
     = (8(4 + 5√3))⁄(2·3)
     = (4(4 + 5√3))⁄3.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Step 6. Conclusion

One may show by a (lengthy) area‐calculation that the pentagon (with vertices A, B, T, C, D in that order) has area 22. (We omit these details.) In any event one may prove that all the conditions force

  [TAD] = (16 + 20√3)⁄3.

Any solution that shows this is correct.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final Answer

The area of triangle TAD is

  (16 + 20√3)⁄3.

Any answer equivalent to this is correct.
